text: Richard Stallman is a computer scientist and software freedom advocate, born in 1953 in New York City. He is best known for founding the GNU Project, a free and open-source software initiative aimed at creating a free operating system compatible with Unix. Stallman introduced the concept of copyleft, a legal mechanism to protect the freedom to modify and redistribute software, first implemented in the GNU Emacs General Public License. He also developed key GNU tools such as the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC), GNU Debugger (GDB), and GNU Make. Stallman has been a vocal critic of proprietary software and has advocated for software freedom as a moral and ethical imperative, arguing that users should have the right to study, modify, and share the software they use. He has promoted the use of terms like "free software" and "open source" to emphasize freedom over proprietary ownership. Stallman is also known for his work on the Free Software Foundation (FSF), which he co-founded and served as president. He has contributed to the development of free software and has been involved in various advocacy efforts, including promoting free software in education and public policy. He has received numerous honors, including the MacArthur Fellowship and the ACM Software System Award. Stallman has also been involved in public debates on software patents, digital rights management, and surveillance. In 2019, he resigned from the FSF and MIT following controversy over his comments on the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, but returned to the FSF board in 2021. He lives in Boston and is known for using free software and open-source tools in his personal life.
